facts.text: I get short of breath when I exert myself.
I get short of breath when I lie flat.

facts.item: waking up at night short of breath
facts.text: I wake up at night short of breath.
It now reaches up to my belly.

facts.item: how long the symptoms have been going on
facts.text: All of this started about a week ago.
Four weeks ago I had heart bypass surgery, with grafts to two arteries (the LAD and the posterior descending artery).
In the same operation my aortic valve was replaced with a tissue (bioprosthetic) valve.
I have coronary artery disease in several arteries.
Before the valve replacement I had severe aortic stenosis.
I have paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that comes and goes.

facts.item: disease of the lining around the heart
facts.text: I've never had any problem with the sac around my heart.
I've never had heart muscle disease.
I don't have any autoimmune conditions.
I've never noticed any symptoms from my heart rhythm.

findings.name: peripheral oedema
findings.result: Pitting oedema extending to the abdomen.

findings.name: lung examination
findings.result: Reduced breath sounds at both lung bases.

findings.name: chest radiograph
findings.result: Bilateral pleural effusions without pericardial calcification.

findings.name: electrocardiography
findings.result: Sinus rhythm without ischaemic changes or low-voltage QRS complexes.

findings.name: transthoracic echocardiography
findings.result: Normal chamber sizes; preserved left ventricular systolic function; normal prosthetic valve function; no regional wall-motion abnormalities. Bright, thickened pericardium with a small pericardial effusion. Dilated inferior vena cava without respirophasic collapse. Respirophasic septal motion (septal bounce) indicating ventricular interdependence. Mitral inflow velocity varies by > 25% with respiration and tricuspid inflow velocity by > 40%.

gold.reasoning: 1. Acute left ventricular dysfunction was considered but deemed unlikely — “there was no clear precipitant for this identified from the patient’s clinical history.” 2. Acute valvular pathology was considered but made less likely — “although no murmur was identified on clinical exam.” 3. Uncontrolled tachyarrhythmias were considered but unsupported — “there was no history of palpitations, pre-syncope, or syncope to support this.” 4. Pulmonary embolism or lower respiratory tract infection were considered in the differential — “other diagnostic possibilities included superimposed pulmonary pathology such as pulmonary embolism or lower respiratory tract infection.” 5. Constrictive pericarditis was suspected based on echocardiographic features — “Note was made of a bright, thickened pericardium, and a small pericardial effusion… Respirophasic septal motion (septal bounce) consistent with ventricular interdependence was also noted.”
